newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish life assurance sector suffers low growth.
newsitem.headline: Irish life assurance sector suffers low growth.

text.p: The Irish life assurance market has seen the lowest growth rate of any major European country over the last five years, a new study showed.
The study, launched on Monday by Dublin-based strategy consultants Prospectus, found that consumer confidence had been shaken by poor investment performance and lack of transparency.
It also showed that new business growth rates had slowed to a trickle with a mere 0.5 percent increase in new life business in 1994, the latest year for which statistics were available.

"If you exclude pensions, then the fall-off in new life business has continued into 1996 with consumer trust shaken by poor investment performance, lack of transparency and in many cases inadequate service levels," Prospectus said.

The report also found a sustained decline in new business levels in Ireland over the last five years, a period when competition escalated. New business fell by 16 percent between 1990 and 1994 to 719 million Irish pounds.

Despite speculation that deregulation could mean an influx of overseas competitors, the study found that there was no prospect of a large number of new entrants coming into the Irish market which is already overcrowded.
A total of 31 life offices compete in what is a small market by European standards and only 15 out of the 31 firms have a market share in excess of one percent.
Prospectus said a market share of five to eight percent was seen as essential for long-term survival and to avoid losing money on new business.

It expects the life market to gravitate toward the bancassurance groups and four or five major life offices and notes that industry sources predict that the number of life offices could fall to as few as eight over the next decade.

Prospectus warned that the life assurance industry could not afford to be complacent about the need to increase the degree of transparency regarding pricing and investment performance if it was to maintain the trust and confidence of consumers in the longer term.

"Our findings show clearly that the life assurance sector in Ireland is at a crossroads," Prospectus managing director David Duffy said. "For too long the industry has been characterised by me-too strategies with little innovation. There is a need for wholesale product reinvention if consumer needs are to be met, even in the short term,"

He said companies must examine product and service strategies in retailing, airlines and tourism as well as paying much close attention to the strategic innovation occurring in life markets elsewhere in Europe such as the Netherlands.
